Question: Regarding the theory of gradual evolution, how can populations of partially evolved individuals survive their "death sentence" of being handicapped? Isn't evolution the "survival of the fittest"? The partially evolved animal is easy prey, right?
Old_Answer: Wrong. You see, the whole “partially evolved” idea is wrong. At every point, you have an animal which is a slight improvement on what came before. A well-known example is the eye. You start out with a light-sensitive patch on the skin. This way, the animal can know whether it is in the open (potentially dangerous; something might eat it) or hidden beneath something (safer; it’s harder to find). Two patches is better: you can start to “see” which direction light is coming from, and in which direction it is darker. If the patches are in dimples on the skin, the direction sensing gets much better. If they are in a deep recess, it gets even better and you can even get something like an image of the surroundings, with light and shade. A transparent membrane protects your proto-eyes… and this goes on, until you have fully functioning eyes. Every stage is an improvement. There is no such thing as “partially evolved” – all the proto-eyes are useful, and good enough for the animals’ purposes. And we know this because every time the eye gets improved, there’s a part of the population that stays behind, and they are still around – hiding under rocks, in the case of the light-sensitive patch. It’s good enough if all you want to do is to hide from the light. Those two things – gradual improvement and “good enough” – is what is missing from your description. Every step along the way has to improve on what was already there. But your description actually shows why there are still apes – another thing that mystify people with only the sketchiest knowledge about evolution. If apes tried to evolve into humans – or rather, something “human-like” – now, when we are already around, they’d be out-competed in no time at all. They’d be rather bad at being apes, and rather bad at being humans, and they wouldn’t have a “place” of their own in the ecology to occupy. They’d have to do something different – maybe become carnivorous, or living in water, or something else that humans didn’t do. “Omnivorous, savannah-dwelling tool-wielder” is already taken.
Answer_with_writing_sample: The theory of gradual evolution is often misunderstood as a linear progression toward perfection, but it’s more about the adaptability of species in response to environmental pressures. Yes, evolution is frequently summarized as "survival of the fittest," but fitness is context-dependent. A partially evolved individual may seem handicapped in one situation, but its traits could provide advantages in another. For example, a creature with a less efficient method of locomotion might excel in an environment where speed is less critical than camouflage or resourcefulness. Moreover, the genetic diversity within populations allows different traits to be advantageous under varying circumstances, which means that not every individual needs to be in peak condition to contribute to the gene pool. Think of it this way: the survival of the fittest doesn’t mean the strongest or fastest always win; it means those best suited to their environment do. Additionally, many species are not in a constant state of evolution toward a single "optimal" form but rather fluctuate in traits based on the environmental context. Over time, these gradually evolving characteristics can become advantageous, and the so-called "handicaps" may serve other functions or become advantageous in future scenarios. Therefore, instead of dying out, these partially evolved individuals can survive and even thrive, demonstrating the complexity and resilience of evolutionary processes. The real lesson here is that evolution is not a race; it’s more of a marathon, with many routes to success and survival.

Thus, rather than viewing these individuals as "handicapped," it’s essential to recognize that they may have adapted in ways that allow them to survive and even thrive under certain conditions, illustrating the complex interplay of evolution.

Furthermore, evolution operates over generations, and what may seem like a handicap can be compensated for by other traits or behaviors — think of social structures or cooperative breeding, where individuals contribute to the care of the young despite their own reduced fitness. Hence, survival isn’t solely about individual superiority; it’s also about the dynamics of the entire population and environment. Evolutionary success is a multifaceted concept that encompasses more than just the strength of physical traits; it includes the intricate interplay of genetics, behavior, and environmental adaptability.

Question: In Europe, are the people that convert to Islam usually politically left-wing or right-wing?
Old_Answer: They’re usually politically getting married to a Muslim, which is the only reason I have ever heard of when people convert to Islam, or actually to any religion. Well, there was a Swedish painter some 150 years ago, but he died and his political leanings wouldn’t be hugely relevant today. The real answer is: It’s such a fantastically rare event that no one can collect statistics on it. But more generally, people who follow authoritarian ideologies are more likely to switch to a different authoritarian ideology, even if that ideology is diametrically opposed to the first one. Today, that would mean that followers of right-wing ideologies would be far more likely to convert: the right wing has become increasingly openly authoritarian in Europe, while the authoritarian left wing has been almost completely eradicated. I would expect that the pattern was different 50 years ago.

Question: Of the sci-fi concepts such as faster than light travel, teleportation, and false gravity on space craft (without it spinning), or other, which is the least likely/furthest away?
Old_Answer: That depends on the exact flavour of each of those things. As far as we know, FTL travel throught a “wormhole” is not forbidden by the laws of physics. There might still be an unknown law forbidding it, and it seems a wormhole can’t be stable for long enough to send an object through it, but FTL communication would still be on the cards, as per current knowledge. (Also, we wouldn’t have the faintest clue how to create one, much less manipulate it.) And then we have hypotheticals like the Alcubierre drive, which requires a form of matter we have good reasons to believe doesn’t exist, but no solid evidence against. Teleportation in the shape of the Star Trek “transporter” isn’t as insane as it sounds. What they do is to take you apart atom by atom, scan the exact quantum state of each atom, and then – depending on SF franchise – either send the atoms one by one to be re-assembled at the destination, or just send the information and assemble locally available atoms into an exact copy, indistinguishable even on the atomic level. Absolutely insanely complex, to the point of probably never being possible in practice, but not actually forbidden by the fundamental laws of physics. Whether the copy is actually the same person, though, is a matter for philosophers. (I would tend to say “no”, although I can’t quite articulate why… except by saying you’re never stuffing me inside one of those things.) Artificial gravity is so far off the table that you hardly ever even read about it in SF novels. It only exists in TV and movies, and even so, only as a handwave explanation for why the actors aren’t floating around the room. There is absolutely nothing that would lead us to suspect gravity can be manipulated that way.

Question: Where will the gravity of the Earth be zero?
Old_Answer: There is only one: at the center of the Earth. There, the Earth pulls at you equally in all directions, and the net force is zero. Of course, the center of the Earth is filled with metal at immense temperatures and pressure… but there is no gravity (net; there is gravity all around but it cancels out).
Answer_with_writing_sample: The gravity of the Earth will be zero at a point known as the "Lagrange point," specifically L1, L2, or L3 in the context of the Earth-Moon system or the Earth-Sun system. These are points in space where the gravitational forces of the two larger bodies (like the Earth and the Moon) balance out the centripetal force felt by a smaller object, allowing it to maintain a stable position relative to the larger bodies. So, if you were to find yourself at one of these points, you wouldn't feel the pull of Earth's gravity at all. However, let's clarify that this doesn't mean you can just float around freely without any gravity. In a practical sense, you would still feel the effects of gravity from the remaining celestial bodies in your vicinity, so the sensation of 'zero gravity' is more of a relative term in these scenarios. In other words, you won't be weightless in all contexts, just in relation to the Earth. If you’re hoping to experience this state, you might have to hitch a ride on a space mission to one of these points since they’re located out in the vacuum of space! But remember, it’s not a permanent escape; it's more like a delicate dance in the gravitational ballet of celestial mechanics. So, while standing on Earth, gravity will always have its grip on you.
Answer_with_user_profile: The gravity of the Earth can be considered zero at the Lagrange point known as L1, which is located between the Earth and the Moon. This point is unique in that it creates a balance of gravitational forces, allowing an object placed there to maintain a stable position relative to both celestial bodies. While the intense gravitational pull of the Earth diminishes as you move further away into space, it never truly reaches a state of zero gravity until you consider points where the gravitational influences of other celestial bodies come into play. For example, at the L2 point, which exists on the opposite side of the Earth from the Moon, one could experience microgravity conditions, but the force is not entirely null. It’s fascinating to note that while we often refer to 'zero gravity' in casual discussions, what we truly mean is a state of microgravity, where the effects of gravity are significantly less than what we experience on Earth's surface. This understanding is crucial, especially in fields such as astrophysics and aerospace engineering, where the behavior of matter in low-gravity environments is pivotal for research and exploration. Thus, while we can find points in space where gravitational effects are minimized, true 'zero' gravity is more of an ideal than a physical reality in the universe that we inhabit.
Answer_with_full_information: The gravity of the Earth will never truly reach zero in any practical sense, as gravity is a universal force that acts on all objects with mass. However, there are specific locations in space where the effects of Earth's gravity can be effectively neutralized or countered. A prime example is the Lagrange points, particularly L1, L2, and L3, where the gravitational pull of the Earth and other celestial bodies, like the Moon or the Sun, balance out in such a way that an object placed there can maintain a stable position relative to those bodies. At these points, the gravitational forces and the centrifugal force of an object's orbit are in perfect equilibrium. This creates a sensation of weightlessness for an object or an astronaut located at these points. Moreover, when in orbit around the Earth—like the astronauts aboard the International Space Station (ISS)—the sensation of weightlessness is experienced due to freefall; the station and everything in it are in constant freefall towards the Earth while simultaneously moving forward at high speeds. This situation creates an environment where the effects of gravity are not felt in the same way they are on the surface. So, while you can find areas where gravity's influence is significantly reduced, it’s never actually zero, as the fundamental pull of Earth’s mass is always present, just less perceptible under certain conditions.

Question: What is your review of Rebel Moon Zack Snyder's movie (Netflix)?
Old_Answer: I watched the first one. It was so bad I have no intention of ever watching the second one. If you want specifics, it was a clumsy pilot episode for a live action version of a manga written by someone who had heard about manga but never read one. The characters were cartoonish, the scenes so clumsily plagiarised that I could name the original movie scene for about 2/3 of the running time, and the narrative structure very much reminiscent of the cartoons I read when I was 10 – they just ran around a few places basically collecting members of the Village People, the movie ending when they had the full set. I’m in an SF fan group on Facebook. The consensus verdict was that it had been marketed as “Star Wars for grown-ups”, but in reality it was “Star Wars for children”. Prequel issue, that is.
Answer_with_writing_sample: Rebel Moon is an ambitious project that showcases Zack Snyder's signature visual flair but struggles with narrative coherence. The film, which is clearly a love letter to the space opera genre, boasts stunning cinematography and some impressive world-building. However, it often feels like Snyder is throwing every idea he has at the screen without fully developing them. The characters, while visually intriguing, lack depth; you get the sense that they exist more as vehicles for action sequences than as fully realized individuals. The pacing can be erratic, oscillating between breathtaking action and drawn-out exposition that doesn’t quite land. It’s almost as if Snyder is trying to fit an entire trilogy’s worth of plot into one film, which leads to rushed moments that could have benefited from more breathing room. Fans of Snyder’s work might appreciate the aesthetic and the bold visuals, but those looking for a tightly woven narrative might find themselves disappointed. The film has all the trappings of a grand sci-fi saga – epic battles, alien races, and moral dilemmas – but it occasionally feels like it’s trying too hard to emulate the giants of the genre without finding its own voice. In a nutshell, Rebel Moon is a visually arresting experience that will likely provoke a mix of admiration and frustration, depending on whether you prioritize style over substance. If Snyder can hone in on character development in future installments, he might just create something truly memorable.
